To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ceramic water filter is a promising technology that has been shown to reduce the incidence of diarrhoea, but the use of these filters is declining over time.

1) the ceramic water filter is a viable technology for household water treatment in rural Cambodia, 2) filter use is sustained over time, and 3) filter use is correlated with water, sanitation, and hygiene practices and with the household's investment in the technology.

ceramic water filters were used in rural Cambodia for 3 years on average after implementation, with the rate of decline in use largely attributable to breakages; filter use was associated with the presence of related water, sanitation, and hygiene practices in households; and the use of surface water was the strongest correlate of continued filter use.

The main takeaway from our work is that
, while ceramic water filters may be a useful intervention for households in rural Cambodia, the technology will not be effective if the filters are not used.
